data.title: 3D Micro-concrete Hybrid Structures Fabricated by Femtosecond Laser Two-Photon Polymerization for Biomedical and Photonic Applications
data.Journal: IEEE International Conference on Industrial Technology
Affiliations: National University of Singapore, 4 Engineering Drive 3, 117576, Singapore
State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies for Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China

data.Abstract: How to fabricate micro-scale 3D structures with an efficient method is the key issue to achieve many long-pursuit exciting goals, such as direct 3D printing to make human organs and fabrication of integrated photonic circuits. Two-photon polymerization (2PP) is more competitive than other 3D printing methods because it is the unique approach capable to acquire around 100 nm resolution to fabricate tiny structures, which are fundamental components in these applications. However, the photoresist used in this method lacks the key material properties to fulfill the requirements of such applications, including mechanical strength and light trapping efficiency. In this work, we present two hybrid methods to modify the photoresist into micro-concretes. With such modifications, the key material properties are enhanced, which transfers it into the feasible building blocks to achieve unique functionalities. These improved hybrid micro-concretes offer tunable mechanical strength, light trapping efficiency and flexible design for bio-medical devices and micro-photonic sources, which represent a new paradigm to nano-engineer the mechanical and optical properties for various applications.
Objective: Core goal: Modify 2PP photoresist into micro-concrete to enhance mechanical and light-trapping properties, and expand applications in biomedicine and photonics.
Develop hybrid two-photon polymerization to achieve this modification.
Achieve precise control of mechanical strength and develop photonic devices.
Overcome functional limitations of conventional 2PP photoresist and realize customized regulation of submicron 3D structures.
Simultaneously enhance the luminescence performance of materials.
Novelty: First proposed the concept of 'micro-concrete' to achieve multifunctional modification of photoresist.
Young's modulus can be tuned by ±22%, with a maximum increase of 70%.
Proposed two hybrid strategies for customized performance modification.
Compatible with full-function manufacturing of biological structures and photonic devices on the same processing platform.
High resolution and biocompatibility for artificial organs and sensor applications.
Simple and efficient doping process for rapid preparation of hybrid photoresists.
Bio-inspired micro-concrete design for simultaneous mechanical and optical functionalization.
Reversible modulus regulation for multi-functional materials in one system.
Tunable light trapping via gold nanoparticle size and low-loss active luminescent waveguides.
Processing resolution up to ~120 nm, far exceeding traditional 3D printing.
Method: Core process: Femtosecond laser two-photon polymerization (2PP) with 800 nm femtosecond laser source.
Material modification: Dope photoresist with silica, gold nanoparticles and Rhodamine 6G.
Performance characterization: AFM, optical spectroscopy and fluorescence measurements.
Material preparation: Mix nanoparticles with IP-L photoresist to prepare three functional hybrid photoresists.
Post-processing: Development with PGMEA + IPA.
Supplementary characterization: SEM morphology and transmission spectroscopy.
Parameter optimization: Test 8.4-270 mW and 30 μm/s-5 mm/s processing parameters.
Performance Metrics: Processing resolution up to ~120 nm.
Young's modulus tunable range ±22%, maximum improvement 70%.
Gold nanoparticles show characteristic absorption peaks at 616 nm (10 nm) and 651 nm (30 nm).
Characteristic fluorescence of Rhodamine 6G at 560 nm under 532 nm pumping.
Optimal parameters: 8.4 mW power, 30 μm/s scanning speed.
Rapid direct writing of large-area structures up to 0.5×0.5 mm².
Processing structure thickness < 5 μm.

data.title: Synthetic waves sensor enables turbulence-resistant imaging
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Field Manipulation Science and Technology, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
Research Center on Vector Optical Fields, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
College of Materials Science and Opto-Electronic Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
data.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence severely distorts optical wavefronts, posing a major obstacle to high-fidelity imaging in automobiles, astronomical observation, and remote sensing. Accurate measurement of the phase distribution across the turbulence field is therefore essential for mitigating its deleterious effects. However, the central challenge lies in acquiring transmission matrices at different depths along the propagation path. Maintaining high precision in three-dimensional phase detection remains challenging for existing techniques. Furthermore, the intricate optical configurations in these techniques often lead to bulky system designs and high costs, limiting their effectiveness in complex turbulence environments. To overcome this limitation, we present a Synthetic waves sensor (SWS) capable of real-time and three-dimensional phase measurement. This system enables compensation for atmospheric turbulence effects to reconstruct objects embedded deep within turbulence. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the utility of SWS by imaging target object through four layers turbulence. The structural similarity index (SSIM) of the reconstruction image improves significantly from 56% to 83%, indicating a high enhancement in image fidelity—from barely visible to clearly resolved targets. Our findings introduce a transformative framework for three-dimensional turbulence characterization and correction, offering promising applications in deep optical imaging under adverse environmental conditions.
Objective: Core objective: Realize real-time 3D phase measurement of atmospheric turbulence, compensate for turbulence distortion, and achieve high-fidelity turbulence-resistant imaging.
Solve the problems that traditional sensors (Shack-Hartmann, LIDAR) cannot distinguish longitudinal turbulence distribution and have limited accuracy and real-time performance.
Overcome the limitations of existing technologies that are difficult to balance 3D detection, system compactness and real-time performance.
Verify the effectiveness of the new SWS sensor and improve optical imaging quality in complex turbulence environments.
Novelty: Realize depth-resolved 3D phase detection along the optical axis, breaking the limitation that traditional technologies can only measure integrated phase.
Compact system structure, only requiring a synthetic wave module and two photodetectors, easy to integrate into existing optical platforms.
After turbulence correction, imaging SSIM increases from 56% to 83%, significantly improving image quality.
Common-path design has high anti-interference ability and naturally shields flow field interference in non-region of interest.
Realize real-time 3D reconstruction of dynamic turbulence fields.
Support metasurface lens integration with further miniaturization potential.
Method: Core scheme: Split the beam to generate two coherent sub-waves, and form synthetic wave interference through AOM frequency shift.
Use four-layer turbulence phase screen for numerical simulation to verify the turbulence correction effect.
Evaluate the quality of imaging reconstruction by calculating SSIM.
Form an interference sensitive area in the focused area to realize phase difference detection of local turbulence.
Use transfer matrix theory and inverse operation for image restoration and correction.
Use dual avalanche photodetectors (APD) to collect interference signals and invert phase information.
Simulate the free-space propagation of light waves combined with the angular spectrum propagation model.
Performance Metrics: Phase detection error <±0.006 (normalized wavelength), the mean value of 40 independent experiments is close to zero, with excellent repeatability.
After turbulence correction, imaging SSIM increases from 56% to 83.
Phase detection resolution better than 0.001 (normalized wavelength).
High system phase sensitivity, a small phase shift of 0.1 rad can produce obvious waveform modulation.
System operating wavelength is 1064 nm, and diffraction-limited imaging resolution can be achieved after correction.
The simulated turbulence layer is located at a depth of 880-1120 mm, suitable for deep turbulence detection requirements.

data.title: A frozen matrix hybrid optical nonlinear system enhanced by a particle lens
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, National University of Singapore, 4 Engineering Drive 3, 117576, Singapore
Centre for Micro-Photonics and CUDOS, Faculty of Science, Engineering and Technology, Swinburne University of Technology, Hawtorn, VIC 3122, Australia
data.Abstract: In this work, a Graphene Oxide (GO) nano-sheet and SiO2 micro-bead hybrid system based on a frozen matrix was investigated for its enhanced optical nonlinear performance. A frozen matrix is a novel approach that hosts the optical nonlinear nano-particles, which combines the strengths from both liquid and solid phase systems for high performance photonic applications. SiO2 micro-beads were used to induce a local field enhancement effect that improved the optical nonlinearity of GO nano-sheets. The nonlinear performance of the hybrid system is several orders higher than the existing GO nano-sheet liquid dispersion. In addition, this frozen matrix and the local field enhancement effect are two facile and versatile methods that can be applied to many types of nano-particle dispersions.
Objective: Core goal: Solve the problems of easy sedimentation and instability in traditional liquid nonlinear systems and poor compatibility in solid-state systems; construct a hybrid frozen matrix system, enhance the optical nonlinear performance of graphene oxide with SiO₂ particle lenses, and endow the system with self-healing and laser damage resistance.
Meet the performance requirements of high-power laser devices
Achieve high-concentration, non-aggregated high-performance nonlinear optical devices
Novelty: First combine frozen matrix and particle lens to construct a new hybrid nonlinear system, with both high compatibility of liquid and stability of solid state.
Realize self-healing through matrix phase transition, resist high-power laser damage, and fully recover performance after cooling.
SiO₂ particle lens achieve >25-fold local optical field enhancement, greatly improving nonlinear response.
Frozen state fixes particle positions, breaks through high-concentration dispersion bottleneck, and suppresses aggregation and sedimentation.
This strategy is universal and compatible with various nonlinear materials such as metals, semiconductors, and thermally sensitive organics.
Method: Sample preparation: Prepare GO by modified Hummers method, co-disperse with SiO₂ microbeads, then rapidly solidify with dry ice to form frozen matrix.
Simulation: Use FDTD method to simulate local field enhancement of SiO₂ microbeads at 800 nm wavelength.
Performance characterization: Use 800 nm femtosecond laser combined with open-aperture Z-scan technique to test nonlinear absorption properties.
Analyze matrix phase transition behavior under different laser fluences based on dynamic thermal melting theory.
Measure saturable absorption characteristics by input-output energy method.
Compare test results with existing literature data to verify performance improvement.
Performance Metrics: Local optical intensity enhancement >25 times
Nonlinear absorption coefficient increased from -0.65×10⁴ cm/GW (pure GO) to -1.31×10⁴ cm/GW (GO+SiO₂), with an increase of 101.5%
At 3.4 μJ/cm², normalized transmittance peak: 1.19 for pure GO, 1.52 for GO+SiO₂
Nonlinear performance improved by several orders of magnitude compared with traditional GO aqueous dispersion
System can withstand laser fluence up to 5.0 μJ/cm² with no performance decay after melting and cooling
Focused volume of SiO₂ microbeads is about 1.01 μm³

data.title: A planar chiral meta-surface for optical vortex generation and focusing
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies on Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
data.Abstract: Data capacity is rapidly reaching its limit in modern optical communications. Optical vortex has been explored to enhance the data capacity for its extra degree of freedom of angular momentum. In traditional means, optical vortices are generated using space light modulators or spiral phase plates, which would sharply decrease the integration of optical communication systems. Here we experimentally demonstrate a planar chiral antenna array to produce optical vortex from a circularly polarized light. Furthermore, the antenna array has the ability to focus the incident light into point, which greatly increases the power intensity of the generated optical vortex. This chiral antenna array may have potential application in highly integrated optical communication systems.
Objective: Core goal: Solve the problems of large volume and low integration of traditional optical vortex devices (spiral phase plate, SLM); design a planar chiral metasurface to realize the integrated function of optical vortex (OAM) generation and beam focusing.
Overcome the defects of low efficiency and serious co-polarization crosstalk of early single-layer metasurfaces, and improve the data capacity and integration of optical communication systems.
Verify the effectiveness of the novel metasurface device and realize compact high-performance photonic devices.
Novelty: Integrated function: First realize OAM generation and focusing simultaneously on a single-layer planar device, compressing traditional discrete components into an ultra-thin structure.
High efficiency: Cross-polarization conversion efficiency >40%, significantly exceeding the 25% theoretical limit of traditional single-layer metasurfaces, without additional polarization filtering.
Ultra-thin and integrable: Device thickness <λ/4, with high on-chip integration potential.
Bidirectional reversible operation: Based on optical reciprocity, it can convert planar light into focused vortex light and point source into collimated OAM beam.
High signal-to-noise ratio: Co-polarized components do not participate in focusing, pure focal plane signal, naturally suppressing crosstalk.
Method: Structure design: Design a hexagonal close-packed array of elliptical silver nanoantennas, and realize 0-2π Pancharatnam-Berry phase control by rotating antenna orientation.
Simulation optimization: Use CST Microwave Studio for full-wave electromagnetic simulation to optimize antenna size and period parameters.
Sample fabrication: Magnetron sputtering of silver film, combined with focused ion beam (FIB) etching to prepare samples.
Performance characterization: Use 633 nm He-Ne laser and build a self-built microscopic system to test transmitted light field distribution.
Phase surface design: Integrate focusing and vortex phase control simultaneously through the phase formula Φ(r,θ)=k√(r²+f²)+lθ.
Performance Metrics: Energy conversion efficiency >40% at 633 nm operating wavelength.
Successfully generate OAM beams with topological charge l=1 and l=2, verifying the flexibility of phase control.
Measured focal length ~23 μm, hollow focal spot radius <1.8 μm.
Effective working bandwidth ~500-656 nm, cross-polarization transmittance is better than co-polarization in this range.
In reverse operation, collimated beam divergence angle is only 6°, verifying bidirectional function.
Antenna parameters: major axis 220 nm, minor axis 66 nm, array period 280 nm, effective radius of metasurface 20 μm.

data.title: A refractory metamaterial absorber for ultra-broadband, omnidirectional and polarization-independent absorption in the UV-NIR spectrum
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies on Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
data.Abstract: In this paper, efficient ultra-broadband absorption from ultraviolet (UV) to near infrared (NIR) is achieved using a metamaterial perfect absorber (MPA) with refractory constituents. Both simulated and experimental results indicate that this proposed MPA exhibits an average absorption over 95% at wavelengths ranging from 200 nm to 900 nm. Besides, owing to the ultrathin thickness and symmetrical topology of this device, it exhibits great angular tolerance up to 60° independent of the incident polarizations. Excellent thermal stability is also demonstrated at high operation temperatures. The physical origin of the ultra-broadband characteristics is mainly based on diffraction/interference engineering at short wavelengths and the anti-reflection effect at long wavelengths. We believe that such a device may find potential applications ranging from photodetection and photothermal energy conversion to ultraviolet protection and thermophotovoltaics.
Objective: Core goal: Solve the problems of narrow bandwidth, angle/polarization sensitivity, and poor high-temperature resistance of traditional metamaterial absorbers; design refractory-based metamaterial absorbers to achieve ultra-broadband, omnidirectional, polarization-independent, and thermally stable high-efficiency light absorption in UV-NIR (200-900 nm).
Meet application requirements in extreme high-temperature environments such as photothermal conversion, thermophotovoltaics, and UV protection.
Overcome the defects of traditional broadband absorbers such as bulky volume and difficulty in integration.
Novelty: Propose dielectric-semiconductor-metal (SiO₂-SiC-W) three-layer structure, combining diffraction enhancement and gradient anti-reflection mechanisms, breaking bandwidth limits of single resonance to achieve ultra-broadband absorption in 200-900 nm.
Adopt refractory materials and passivation layer design, resistant to 800℃ in air, solving oxidation and structural collapse issues of traditional metamaterials.
Symmetric subwavelength structure enables excellent omnidirectional tolerance and polarization independence, maintaining high absorption at large angles.
Use interference lithography instead of E-beam lithography to achieve low-cost, industrial large-area fabrication compatible with roll-to-roll mass production.

Synergy of three absorption mechanisms: short-wave diffraction enhancement, long-wave anti-reflection, and full-band electric field dissipation in tungsten, enabling high-efficiency full-band absorption.
Method: Structure design: Design periodic tungsten nanocylinder arrays coated with SiC and SiO₂ passivation layers to build subwavelength periodic structures.
Simulation optimization: Use CST Microwave Studio for full-wave electromagnetic simulation to optimize structural parameters.
Sample fabrication: Prepare samples via magnetron sputtering, interference lithography, RIE / ion beam etching.
Performance characterization: Measure reflectivity with ellipsometer, calculate absorptivity by A=1-R, test absorption at different angles and polarizations.
Thermal stability test: High-temperature annealing in air to verify structural and performance stability at elevated temperatures.
Mechanism analysis: Explain long-wave absorption mechanism using effective medium theory and Maxwell-Garnett theory.
Performance Metrics: Average absorptivity >95% in 200-900 nm, covering full UV-Vis-NIR band.
Angle tolerance: Absorptivity >95% at 60° incidence, >90% at 70°, no difference between TE/TM polarizations.
Thermal stability: Almost no change in morphology and absorption after annealing at 600℃ for 1 hour in air.
At 800℃, structure shrinks slightly but remains stable, verifying adaptability to extreme environments.
Structural parameters: Unit period 300 nm, W pillar diameter 120 nm, SiC/SiO₂ layers 40 nm each, total thickness only 80 nm (subwavelength ultra-thin).
Process cost: Interference lithography reduces cost by one order of magnitude, suitable for industrial large-scale production.

data.title: Achromatic flat optical components via compensation between structure and material dispersions
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies on Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
data.Abstract: Chromatism causes great quality degradation of the imaging system, especially for diffraction imaging. The most commonly method to overcome chromatism is refractive/diffractive hybrid optical system which, however, sacrifices the light weight and integration property of diffraction elements. A method through compensation between the structure dispersion and material dispersion is proposed to overcome the chromatism in flat integrated optical components. This method is demonstrated by making use of silver nano-slits waveguides to supply structure dispersion of surface plasmon polaritons (SPP) in metal-insulator-metal (MIM) waveguide to compensate the material dispersion of metal. A broadband deflector and lens are designed to prove the achromatic property of this method. The method demonstrated here may serve as a solution of broadband light manipulation in flat integrated optical systems.
Objective: To overcome chromatic aberration in flat integrated optical components and metasurfaces.
To utilize compensation between structure dispersion and material dispersion to realize achromatic plasmonic components (APC).
To achieve broadband achromatic performance without sacrificing the lightweight and integration properties of diffractive elements.
To design and validate broadband achromatic deflectors and lenses using silver nano-slits waveguides.
Design and validate a broadband achromatic plasmonic deflector and lens operating in the wavelength range 1000-2000 nm.
Design broadband achromatic plasmonic deflector and lens using silver MIM waveguides.
Validate achromatic performance in 1000-2000 nm wavelength range through theory and simulation.
Demonstrate broadband achromatic performance via compensation between structure dispersion of SPP in MIM waveguides and material dispersion of metal.
Novelty: Proposed a method to use structure dispersion of Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SPP) mode in Metal-Insulator-Metal (MIM) waveguides to compensate material dispersion of metal.
Achieved broadband achromatic performance in the range of 1000-2000 nm, unlike previous methods that only worked at discrete wavelengths.
Demonstrated that the achromatic deflector can maintain performance at arbitrary incident angles, superior to dielectric metasurfaces with limited incident angle tolerance.
Provided a theoretical proof and simulation validation of achromatic effect in MIM waveguides under specific frequency conditions.
First demonstration of continuous broadband achromatic operation (not just multi-wavelength) in flat optics via dispersion compensation.
Uses metal-insulator-metal (MIM) waveguides to exploit opposite signs of structure dispersion (from SPP mode) and material dispersion (from metal).
Shows that the product Δφ·λ is dispersionless, enabling achromatic design.
Achieves achromatic deflection at arbitrary incident angles (-10° to 40°) with <5% deviation.
Avoids complex parameter scanning required in prior multi-wavelength metasurface methods.
Deflector maintains achromatism for arbitrary incident angles (-10° to 40°), outperforming dielectric metasurfaces with ±1° tolerance.
First continuous broadband achromatic flat components (1000-2000 nm) using MIM waveguides, outperforming prior discrete-wavelength metasurface designs.
Eliminates complex parameter scanning required in previous dispersive phase compensation methods.
Method: Theoretical analysis of dispersion properties of silver MIM waveguides using eigenvalue equation and Drude model.
Numerical simulations using COMSOL 4.3 with Perfect Matched Layer (PML) as absorbing boundary condition.
Designed achromatic deflector with 29 metallic slits and achromatic lens with 51 metallic slits of varying widths.
Compared phase distributions and electric field intensity at different wavelengths to validate achromatic performance.
Theoretical derivation showing that for MIM waveguides under conditions ω ≪ ω_p and ω ≫ γ, β·λ and thus Δφ·λ are constant.
Design of unit cells with variable slit width (20-100 nm), fixed waveguide length h = 3 μm, period p = 200 nm, silver as metal, air (ε_d=1) as dielectric.
Simulate via COMSOL 4.3 with PML boundaries; silver parameters: ε∞=4.2, ωp=1.3×10¹⁶ rad/s, γ=9.1×10¹³ rad/s.
Deflector design: 29 slits, phase distribution Δφ(x)=-(2π/λ)·x·sinθ_0, targeting θ_0 = -19° at λ=1 μm.
Lens design: 51 slits, phase distribution Δφ(x)=-(2π/λ)(√(x²+f²)-f), targeting f=5 μm.
Theoretical framework: Derive SPP propagation constant β in MIM waveguides via eigenvalue equation, simplified using Drude model for metal permittivity.
Unit cell design: Vary MIM slit width (20-100 nm) with fixed slit depth (3 μm) to tune phase shift while maintaining βλ constant.
Component design: Achromatic deflector arranges slit widths to match phase profile Δφ(x) = -2πx sinθ₀/λ; lens matches Δφ(x) = -2π(√(x²+f²)-f)/λ.
Numerical simulation: Use COMSOL Multiphysics 4.3 with PML boundaries, silver permittivity modeled by Drude parameters (ε∞=4.2, ωₚ=1.3×10¹⁶ rad/s, γ=9.１×１０¹³ rad/s).
Performance Metrics: The deflector maintained achromatic directional radiation with deviation less than 5% at incident angles of -10°, 20°, and 40° across the wavelength range.
The lens achieved a focal length of 5 μm at wavelengths of 1000 nm, 1500 nm, and 2000 nm.
The broadband achromatic performance was demonstrated in the wavelength range of 1000-2000 nm.
The phase shift multiplied by wavelength (Δφ·λ) remained constant at different wavelengths, proving the achromatic property.
Deflector: acheomatic performance maintained for incident angles from -10° to 40°, corresponding to output angles from -35° to37°.
Simulated phase distributions match theoretical predictions (Fig.4b), and Δφ·λ profiles nearly identical across wavelengths (Fig.4c).
Achromatic validation: Δφ·λ remains constant at all spatial positions for both deflector and lens, confirming dispersionless performance.

data.title: All-Dielectric Metasurfaces for Simultaneous Giant Circular Asymmetric Transmission and Wavefront Shaping Based on Asymmetric Photonic Spin-Orbit Interactions
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies on Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Technology and System, Ministry of Education, Chongqing University, Chongqing 400030, China
data.Abstract: The control of polarization and wavefront plays an important role in many optical systems. In this work, a monolayer metasurface is proposed to simultaneously realize circular asymmetric transmission (AT) and wavefront shaping based on asymmetric spin-orbit interactions. Circularly polarized incidence, accompanied with arbitrary wavefront modulation, experiences spin-selected destructive or constructive interference. An extinction ratio of ≈10:1 and an AT parameter of ≈0.69 at 9.6 µm, as well as a full width half-maximum of ≈2.9 µm (≈30% of the peak wavelength), are measured with the designed metasurface. These measured results are more than four times of those achieved with previous monolayer chiral structures. As far as it is known, this is the first report on the realization of simultaneous giant AT and arbitrary wavefront modulation with only one metasurface. Due to its fabrication simplicity and the multifunctionality of the designed metasurface, this work may provide a promising route to replace bulky cascading optical components with only one ultrathin metasurface for chiroptical spectroscopy, chiral imaging, optical communication, and so forth.
Objective: To experimentally realize giant and broadband circular asymmetric transmission (AT) accompanied by wavefront manipulation for transmitted and reflected circularly polarized lights.
To design a monolayer metasurface capable of simultaneous polarization control and arbitrary wavefront modulation based on asymmetric photonic spin-orbit interactions.
To replace bulky cascading optical components (such as polarizers, waveplates, and lenses) with a single ultrathin metasurface to reduce system volume, weight, and cost.
To achieve high-performance AT comparable to 3D chiral metamaterials while maintaining a simple fabrication process.
To simultaneously realize giant circular asymmetric transmission (AT) and wavefront shaping using a single-layer all-dielectric metasurface.
To achieve spin-selective destructive or constructive interference for circularly polarized incidence, enabling both polarization control and arbitrary wavefront modulation.
To replace bulky cascading optical components (polarizers, waveplates, lenses) with one ultrathin metasurface for applications such as chiral imaging and optical communication.
To achieve spin-selected destructive/constructive interference via asymmetric photonic spin-orbit interactions.
To realize multifunctional control of circularly polarized light with a single ultrathin metasurface.
Novelty: First report on the realization of simultaneous giant asymmetric transmission (AT) and arbitrary wavefront modulation using a single monolayer metasurface.
Utilizes asymmetric spin-orbit interactions achieved by merging Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase and waveguide retardation phase, breaking the symmetry of photonic SOIs.
Employs a supercell composed of two pairs of twin nanofins with different anisotropy and a relative rotation angle of π/4, avoiding the complex design of intrinsic chiral antennas.
Demonstrates multifunctional capabilities including anomalous refraction, optical vortex generation, and phase holography, all integrated with high AT performance.
Offers fabrication simplicity via a single step of lithography followed by a single etching process, unlike complex 3D chiral metamaterials.
To achieve spin-selective destructive or constructive interference for circularly polarized incidence, enabling both polarization control and arbitrary wavefront modulation.
AT via supercell collective contribution, avoiding complex intrinsic chiral antenna design.
AT performance 4× higher than prior monolayer chiral structures, comparable to 3D metamaterials.
First demonstration of a single metasurface achieving both giant AT and wavefront shaping, outperforming prior monolayer chiral structures by >4× in AT performance.
Uses asymmetric spin-orbit interactions via merging Pancharatnam-Berry phase and waveguide retardation phase, avoiding complex 3D chiral metamaterial fabrication.
Enables spin-selective destructive/constructive interference for AT while independently modulating transmitted/reflected wavefronts via orientation-controlled PB phase.
Method: Designed a monolayer all-silicon metasurface on a double-sided polished Si wafer using finite element method simulations (CST Microwave Studio).
Utilized asymmetric spin-orbit interactions where the supercell consists of two pairs of nanofins with different dimensions and a π/4 rotation angle to induce phase differences.
Incorporated Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase for wavefront shaping by varying the orientation angle of the nanofins.
Fabricated the device using direct laser writing in resist followed by inductive-coupled plasmonic etching to transfer patterns into Si.
Characterized the Jones matrix and AT parameters using a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer coupled with linear polarizers and superachromatic quarter wave plates.
Experimentally demonstrated three wavefront modulators: a beam deflector, an optical vortex generator, and a phase hologram.
Designed supercell composed of two pairs of twin silicon nanofins with different sizes and relative rotation angle of π/4.
Nanofins act as half-wave plates; phase difference φ=π/2 at central wavelength achieved by dimension tuning (e.g., W1=1.45 µm, L1=3.1 µm, H=6.0 µm).
Characterization: Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer with two linear polarizers and two superachromatic quarter-wave plates; CO₂ laser source for wavefront measurement.
Design supercell with two pairs of twin silicon nanofins (α=π/4 rotation, differing anisotropy).
Design: Supercell composed of two pairs of silicon nanofins with π/4 rotation angle difference, engineered to produce π/2 waveguide phase shift at 9.6 μm.
Simulation: finite element method (CST Microwave Studio) with Floquet port and 98 modes.
Performance Metrics: Performance is more than four times higher than previously reported monolayer planar chiral structures (which had an AT parameter of ~0.15 and FWHM of ~3.5%).
Deflector device showed a contrast ratio of ~16:1 between +1st and -1st order diffractions with efficiencies of 67.4% (±1st order), 10.8% (0th order), and 4.2% (-1st order).
Vortex generator successfully produced pure donut-shape patterns with a topological charge of l=+2.
Hologram device generated distinct images (goldfish) in transmission and reflection fields without conjugate image disturbance.
Extinction ratio: ≈10:1 at 9.6 µm (measured), simulated maximum ≈17:1.
AT parameter: ≈0.69 at 9.6 µm (measured), FWHM ≈2.9 µm (≈30% of peak wavelength).
Broadband operation: contrast ratios of deflector from 9.3 µm to 10.6 µm ranged from 11.1 to 18.2.
Vortex generator: topological charge l=+2; hologram eliminates conjugate image disturbance.
Measured extinction ratio ≈10:1, AT parameter ≈0.69 at 9.6 μm; full width half-maximum (FWHM) of AT ≈2.9 μm (~30% of peak wavelength).

data.title: Plasmonic Metasurfaces for Simultaneous Thermal Infrared Invisibility and Holographic Illusion
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Optical Technologies on Nano-Fabrication and Micro-Engineering, Institute of Optics and Electronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610209, China
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
data.Abstract: In 1860s, Gustav Kirchhoff proposed his famous law of thermal radiation, setting a fundamental contradiction between the infrared reflection and thermal radiation. Here, for the first time an ultrathin plasmonic metasurface is proposed to simultaneously produce ultralow specular reflection and infrared emission across a broad spectrum and wide incident angle range by combining the low emission nature of metal and the photonic spin-orbit interaction in spatially inhomogeneous structures. As a proof-of-concept, a phase gradient metasurface composed of sub-wavelength metal gratings is designed and experimentally characterized in the infrared atmosphere window of 8-14 µm, demonstrating an ultralow specular reflectivity and infrared emissivity below 0.1. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that infrared illusion could be generated by the metasurface, enabling not only invisibility for thermal and laser detection, but also multifunctionalities for potential applications. This technology is also scalable across a wide range of electromagnetic spectrum and provides a feasible alternative for surface coating.
Objective: To propose an ultrathin plasmonic metasurface that simultaneously achieves ultralow specular reflection and low infrared emissivity across a broad spectrum and wide incident angles.
To overcome the fundamental contradiction posed by Kirchhoff 's law (linking high absorption to high emission) by decoupling reflection and emission properties.
To demonstrate a proof-of-concept phase gradient metasurface composed of sub-wavelength metal gratings for the 8-14 µm infrared atmospheric window.
To enable multifunctionality by demonstrating the metasurface's capability for infrared illusion, specifically achieving invisibility against both thermal and laser detection.
To demonstrate infrared illusion, enabling thermal and laser detection invisibility, as well as multifunctional reflective optical components such as holograms.
To provide a mechanically robust, all-metallic alternative to traditional lossy dielectric or complex multilayer metamaterials.
Develop scalable all-metallic metasurface for multifunctional electromagnetic manipulation.
Propose an ultrathin plasmonic metasurface for simultaneous ultralow specular reflection and infrared emission.
Realize thermal infrared invisibility and holographic illusion in 8-14 µm atmospheric window.

data.Abstract: Multispectral complementary detection technologies have made single-band camouflage materials ineffective, creating strong demand for multispectral compatible camouflage materials. Here, multiscale-hierarchical metasurfaces (MHM) compatible with large-area low-cost fabrication are proposed for the first time to realize multispectral camouflage of dual-band lasers, infrared and microwave. The MHM consists of an all-metallic metasurface array (AMMA) and a microwave absorber. The AMMA hinders dual-band lasers and thermal infrared detection, while the microwave absorber beneath the AMMA is applied as a defence against microwave detection. As a proof-of-concept, a MHM sample with an area of 30 × 30 cm2 and a minimum linewidth of 1.8 µm is fabricated based on nanoimprint lithography. The excellent multispectral camouflage performance is verified in experiments, showing low reflectance (<0.2) in 0.9-1.2 µm and 9-12 µm, low infrared emissivity (<0.2), and high absorption efficiency of over 90% 2.7-26 GHz. Wide-angle and polarization-independent characteristics are also demonstrated. This work offers a promising opportunity for the engineering application of metasurfaces in the multispectral camouflage field. Moreover, this methodology can be easily extended to other electromagnetic spectrum, providing significant guidance for the design and fabrication of multispectral devices.

data.Abstract: Sorting orbital angular momentum (OAM) and spin angular momentum (SAM) of photons is crucial for optical communications, optical storage, and quantum information processing, wherein complicated optical setups or bulky devices are conventionally utilized to determine the angular momentum via repetitive interference or diffractive projection measurements. Recently, advancements in compact and single-shot OAM detection have been made via coordinate transformation metasurfaces. Nevertheless, most of these strategies require precise separation and alignment between multiple components and cannot simultaneously distinguish full angular momentum states. Besides, the single-shot maximum identifiable OAM mode numbers are generally limited to 60 due to the tradeoff between the mode space and reduced-cross-talk mode interval. Here, this work puts forward and experimentally demonstrates a monolithic spiral metalens (SML) for ultrahigh-capacity sorting full angular momentum states. The SML focus the incident vortex beam into multiple-turn spiral ring rather than a circle ring on the focal plane according to its topological charge, with the mode order ranging from -250 to 250. Consequently, the maximum identifiable OAM mode number is up to 168 under a single-shot measurement, which largely surpass the best results reported hitherto. The experimental results obtained in the telecom band underpin the design approach, which may find great potential in high-capacity communication and storage applications.

data.Abstract: Nonreciprocal transmission based on nonlinear optical materials has attracted considerable attention for eliminating the need for complex and bulky external bias systems and shows great potential for high-intensity laser protection. Strongly resonant structures are commonly used to achieve lower laser operating power and higher efficiency. However, this approach typically compromises other critical performance metrics, such as protection power range, maximum operating power, bandwidth, and angular range. Here, a novel strategy is proposed using weakly resonant structures to realize nonreciprocity while preserving high performance across these metrics. This achievement stems from the large out-of-plane refractive index asymmetry in the Si/VO2 catenary structure, enabling robust nonreciprocal transmission with high efficiency across a broad bandwidth (8-11.5 µm) and angular range (>75°) theoretically. This design also shows a higher operating power ceiling and extends the existing tunable nonreciprocal range by an order of magnitude. Experiments validate the tunable nonreciprocal range at 10.6 µm wavelength. Protection capabilities are significantly enhanced through wavefront modulation, offering rapid and effective protection from below the phase transition to above the damage threshold. This work presents a novel paradigm for robust nonreciprocal metasurfaces, with considerable potential for applications in remote sensing, environmental monitoring, biomedicine, and industrial manufacturing.

data.Abstract: Metasurface holography, with its compact structural design and multi-dimensional multiplexing capabilities, has demonstrated great potential in dynamic display and data storage applications. However, the approach of achieving multiplexing by adjusting different properties of the incident light has nearly exhausted the multiplexing dimensions of metasurfaces, severely hindering the development of information-dense planar diffractive optical devices. Here, the concept of cascaded multiplexing channels is introduced, achieving switchable holographic displays through continuous pixel-level lateral displacement between the layers of two closely stacked diffractive optical devices. To achieve this, a progressive optimization algorithm is developed to enhance the efficiency of optimizing phase profiles for each layer. As a proof of concept, a cascaded liquid crystal (LC) platform based on Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase modulation is experimentally demonstrated, supporting up to 12 independent, nearly crosstalk-free holographic display channels. Furthermore, by integrating traditional multiplexing techniques, an optical secret sharing platform is designed and demonstrated, which can achieve secure transmission and storage of high-capacity information. This work introduces a new multiplexing dimension for compact holographic optical devices, with promising applications in the fields of optical storage, display, encryption, and anti-counterfeiting.

data.Abstract: The coupling between photonic spin and orbital angular momenta is significantly enhanced at the subwavelength scale and has found a plethora of applications in nanophotonics. However, it is still a great challenge to make such kind of coupling tunable with multiple states. Here, a versatile metasurface platform based on polyatomic phase-change resonators is provided to realize multiple-state switching of photonic angular momentum coupling. As a proof of concept, three coupling modes, namely, symmetric coupling, asymmetric coupling, and no coupling, are experimentally demonstrated at three different crystallization levels of structured Ge2Sb2Te5 alloy. In practical applications, coded information can be encrypted in asymmetric mode using the spin degree of freedom, while revealing misleading one without proper phase change or after excessive crystallinity. With these findings, this study may open an exciting direction for subwavelength electromagnetics with unprecedented compactness, allowing to envision applications in active nanophotonics and information security engineering.
Objective: Breaking the limitation that the traditional photonic spin-orbit interaction (PSOI) can only realize on/off two-state switching, this work achieves tunable angular momentum coupling with three or more switchable states for the first time, covering three modes: symmetric coupling, asymmetric coupling and decoupling.

A metasurface architecture based on multi-atom phase-change resonators is proposed. It combines geometric phase and tunable propagation phase to eliminate the drawbacks of traditional interleaved array designs such as pixel loss, severe crosstalk and low efficiency, enabling all units to participate in wavefront manipulation.
Construct a high-security encoding system by utilizing the changes in optical properties of GST materials with different crystallinity levels.

The research is not limited to theoretical exploration; it also aims to verify the practical application potential of this technology in optical information storage and encryption through experiments.
Novelty: Break through the binary limitation of PSOI, realize the active switching of three states (symmetric coupling / asymmetric coupling / no coupling) by utilizing the amorphous, semi-crystalline and fully crystalline states of GST, with the first verification completed.
Propose a new hybrid method combining geometric phase and tunable propagation phase.
Precisely control the semicrystalline GST to achieve asymmetric coupling.

Construct dual-dimensional encryption based on spin polarization and crystallinity of phase-change materials: the amorphous state outputs misleading information, the semi-crystalline state enables multi-channel decoding, and the fully crystalline state scatters noise. Decryption requires matching polarization and thermally induced phase transition.
Infrared-band MIM-structured metasurfaces leveraging the high refractive index contrast and stability of GST.

Fully Reusable and Highly Integrated Metasurface: No pixel loss, elimination of interleaved subarrays, full-unit wavefront manipulation, solving problems such as pixel loss, low fidelity and poor energy efficiency.
Performance Innovation: Full Unit Reuse & High Integration, Breaking Traditional Limitations.
Method: Derive the phase response of reflective anisotropic meta-atoms based on the Jones matrix, and illustrate the coupling relationship between the geometric phase (-2σξ) and the propagation phase (φ).
Electromagnetic theory reveals the SAM-OAM coupling mechanism of photons and analyzes the crystal-state dependent optical response of GST (Ge₂Sb₂Te₅).
Optimize dimer GST resonators via CST simulation to achieve high polarization conversion efficiency in amorphous/semi-crystalline states and eliminate anisotropy in fully crystalline states.
EBE and EBL are used for micro-nano fabrication of GST metasurfaces, while SEM and AFM are adopted to characterize the structural precision.
Programmable annealing regulates the crystalline state of GST. A spectrometer combined with a polarization system verifies the switching between symmetric/asymmetric coupling and off modes.

Irradiation with CO₂ laser, far-field diffraction is recorded by an infrared detector after imaging through a Fourier lens. The OAM topological charge is determined by the interference fringes of oblique circularly polarized light, and the energy efficiency is measured by a power meter.

Observe the microscopic morphology via SEM, characterize orbital angular momentum (OAM), diffraction spots and encrypted imaging using infrared detectors combined with oblique beam interference, test energy efficiency and bandwidth, and verify the scalability of VO₂.
10.6 μm laser system tests OAM topology and holographic imaging to verify the triple encryption of 'symmetric deception - asymmetric encryption - full crystal failure'.

Wavelength: 10.6 μm (CO₂ laser), effective bandwidth Δλ/λ = 10%.
Material deformation: Amorphous to semi-crystalline decreases by 3.4%, amorphous to fully crystalline decreases by 6.9%, with no loss in performance.
Realize the three states of photon angular momentum coupling (symmetric / asymmetric / off).
Phase modulation 0-2π (12 levels ≈ π/6).
Experimentally controllable generation of OAM topological charges l=±2 and l=+1/-3, supporting arbitrary encoding.

Structure: Unit period 5 μm, GST fin height 1 μm, gold layer thickness 0.2 μm (top) / 300 nm (bottom).

data.title: Extreme-Angle Silicon Infrared Optics Enabled by Streamlined Surfaces

data.Abstract: Infrared optical systems are indispensable in almost all domains of society, but their performances are often restricted by bulky size, small field of view, large thermal sensitivity, high fabrication cost, etc. Here, based on the concept of catenary optics, a novel isophase streamline optimization approach is leveraged to design silicon complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible metasurfaces with broadband, wide-angle, and high-efficiency performances, which breaks through the glass ceiling of traditional optical technologies. By using the truly local geometric phase, a maximum diffraction efficiency approaching 100% is obtained in ultrawide spectral and angular ranges. Somewhat surprising results are shown in that wide-angle diffraction-limited imaging and laser beam steering can be realized with a record field of view up to 178°. This methodology is scalable to the entire optical band and other materials, enabling unprecedented compact infrared systems for surveillance, unmanned vehicles, medical science, etc.
Objective: The ultimate goal of this research is to break the 'glass ceiling' of traditional optical technologies and develop an innovative design strategy based on Streamlined Metasurfaces. It aims to construct ultra-compact, ultra-wide-field, high-efficiency and broadband silicon-based infrared optical systems to replace the bulky and limited traditional infrared lenses.

Development of high-performance planar optical devices: Design and fabricate streamlined silicon-based metalenses, achieving diffraction-limited infrared imaging with a record-breaking field of view of 178°, and laser beam scanning at extreme angles exceeding 170°.

Build an integrated infrared imaging system: develop a long-wave/near-infrared integrated super camera to realize thermal imaging, chiral polarization imaging, day-and-night active/passive imaging, and reach the imaging resolution limit of infrared detectors.

Leveraging silicon-based CMOS-compatible processes, we integrate high-performance infrared optics with microelectronic platforms to support the development of compact, low-power and highly stable optical systems for unmanned aerial vehicles, automotive vision, night vision/thermal imaging, satellite remote sensing and other fields.
Novelty: Propose a brand-new design strategy: equiphase streamline optimization.
Breakthrough in performance indicators: Breaking the physical limits of planar optical devices.
Material and Process Innovation: Fully silicon CMOS compatible.
Innovation and Integrated Application of Infrared Optical Systems.
Elimination of parasitic phase: Local streamline width modulation cancels the propagation phase, enabling pure geometric phase control while suppressing stray light and high-order diffraction.

In the 8-14 μm LWIR band, the OSM surpasses conventional, phase-quantized, and discrete metasurfaces in spectral/angular bandwidths and diffraction efficiency, while exhibiting excellent angular robustness.
This versatile approach extends to full optical bands and various dielectrics, supporting large-area 2D and cascaded systems as a general platform for high-performance planar infrared optics.
Method: Based on catenary optics and geometric phase theory, the phase distribution of the streamline structure is derived by means of Jones matrix, vector field differential equations and numerical integration.

Propose an optimization strategy for equiphase streamlines: generate structures via differential equations, dynamically adjust local widths to counteract parasitic phases, and achieve pure geometric phase modulation .

Simulation Design: Analyze polarization conversion and diffraction efficiency using Jones matrix / Floquet theory, and simulate and optimize silicon-based streamlined structures for 8-14 μm long-wave infrared band.
Experimental preparation: Silicon-based streamlined metasurface samples are fabricated using CMOS technology (direct-write lithography + ICP etching).

Experimental Characterization: Verify the consistency between simulation and measured results by combining SEM morphology, far-field diffraction and MTF analysis with beam scanning, infrared thermal imaging and chiral imaging.
Performance Metrics: Field of View (FOV): 178° for single-chip diffraction-limited imaging (hemispherical coverage), laser scanning range ±85°.
Diffraction Efficiency: 98.4%/96.6% at normal incidence, 95.7%/92.6% at 60° oblique incidence, and still above 90% at -85°.
Thermal stability: The geometric phase mechanism eliminates the temperature sensitivity of silicon's refractive index and achieves athermal defocusing-free performance.
Beam deflection > 170° (Applicable to LiDAR)(千问)
Process Compatibility: Feature size ≥ 1μm, compatible with silicon-based CMOS and suitable for large-area fabrication.
Operating wavelength band: Long-wave infrared 8-14μm (atmospheric window), near-infrared up to 940nm.
Imaging Performance: Focal length 5.12mm, radius 6mm; Resolution 29.41 lp/mm (matching the cut-off frequency of the detector).

Structural parameters: Long-wave infrared streamlines with a height of 4.7 μm (7 μm for discrete metasurfaces), minimum feature size of 1 μm; For the 10.6 μm wavelength with 45° deflection, the period is approximately 15 μm (10.6/sin45°).
Wide-angle lens specifications: Focal length 5.12mm/6.5mm, radius 6mm/12.7mm; Near-infrared focal length 4.48mm, aperture 12mm.
System Performance: Backside anti-reflection and transmittance enhancement by 25%; Thermal imaging distance: 60cm; Array lamp FOV: 0-70°; NIR pixel: 5.5μm×5.5μm.
